# Helper: draw one or more confidence intervals
ci_plot <- function(df, xlab, title, subtitle = NULL, ref = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = est, y = method, colour = method)) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), orientation = "y",
                  width = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_point(size = 3.4) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(hw_blue, hw_green, hw_red)[seq_len(nrow(df))],
                        guide = "none") +
    labs(title = title, subtitle = subtitle, x = xlab, y = NULL) +
    hw_theme
  if (!is.null(ref)) {
    p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = ref, linetype = "dashed", colour = hw_red)
  }
  p
}

::: {.question-card}
### Question $1$

A fisheries officer inspects a random sample of $250$ American lobsters landed at ports along the Northumberland Strait. Of these, $38$ show signs of epizootic shell disease.

1. Identify the population, the observational unit and the "success" outcome.
2. Define the population parameter $p$ in words.
3. Calculate the sample proportion $\hat{p}$.
4. Explain the difference between $\hat{p}$ and $p$.
5. If a second random sample of $250$ lobsters were inspected, would you expect the same value of $\hat{p}$? Explain.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>The <b>population</b> is all American lobsters landed at Northumberland Strait ports (during the inspection period). The <b>observational unit</b> is one lobster. A <b>success</b> is a lobster showing signs of shell disease. "Success" just means the outcome being counted. It is not a good outcome here.</li>
  <li>$p$ is the proportion of <i>all</i> lobsters landed at these ports that show signs of shell disease.</li>
  <li>
  $$\hat{p}=\frac{X}{n}=\frac{38}{250}=\boxed{0.152}$$
  so $15.2\%$ of the sampled lobsters show signs of disease.</li>
  <li>$\hat{p}=0.152$ is a <b>statistic</b>. It is known, calculated from this sample, and would change from sample to sample. $p$ is a <b>parameter</b>. It is a fixed but unknown number describing the whole population. We use $\hat{p}$ to estimate $p$.</li>
  <li>No. A different random sample would almost certainly include different lobsters and give a somewhat different $\hat{p}$. This sample-to-sample variation is described by the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$, which is what confidence intervals and tests account for.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $2$

Suppose that $30\%$ of all white-tailed deer in a large provincial herd carry a particular parasite, so $p=0.30$. A wildlife agency will test a random sample of $n=200$ deer.

1. What are the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$?
2. Check that the sampling distribution is approximately Normal.
3. Find the probability that the sample proportion is greater than $0.35$.
4. Find the probability that the sample proportion is within $0.05$ of the true value $0.30$.
5. How would the standard deviation change if the agency tested $800$ deer instead?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>
  $$\mu_{\hat{p}}=p=\boxed{0.30}\qquad
  \sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{(0.30)(0.70)}{200}}=\boxed{0.0324}$$
  </li>
  <li>The expected counts are $np=200(0.30)=60$ successes and $n(1-p)=200(0.70)=140$ failures. Both are large, so $\hat{p}$ is approximately Normal. The herd is large, so the $10\%$ condition is also reasonable.</li>
  <li>
  $$z=\frac{0.35-0.30}{0.0324}=1.543\qquad P(\hat{p}>0.35)=P(Z>1.543)\approx\boxed{0.0614}$$
  </li>
  <li>By symmetry, $P(0.25<\hat{p}<0.35)=1-2(0.0614)\approx\boxed{0.8772}$. About $88\%$ of samples of $200$ deer would give a sample proportion within $5$ percentage points of the truth.</li>
  <li>The standard deviation is proportional to $1/\sqrt{n}$. Multiplying $n$ by $4$ halves it:
  $$\sqrt{\frac{(0.30)(0.70)}{800}}=\boxed{0.0162}$$
  </li>
</ol>

```{r q2-check, echo=TRUE}
sd_phat <- sqrt(0.30 * 0.70 / 200)
pnorm(0.35, mean = 0.30, sd = sd_phat, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

```{r q2-plot}
g <- seq(0.18, 0.42, length.out = 600)
q2 <- data.frame(p = g, d = dnorm(g, 0.30, sd_phat))

ggplot(q2, aes(p, d)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(q2, p >= 0.35), fill = hw_red, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = hw_blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.30, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.385, y = 3, label = "P = 0.0614", colour = hw_red) +
  labs(title = "Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion",
       subtitle = "p = 0.30, n = 200", x = "Sample proportion", y = "Density") +
  hw_theme
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $3$

A random sample of $640$ little brown bats captured at hibernation sites in Nova Scotia found $112$ with visible signs of white-nose syndrome.

1. Check the conditions for a large-sample confidence interval.
2. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion of bats with visible signs.
3. Interpret the interval in context.
4. Construct a $99\%$ confidence interval.
5. Explain why the $99\%$ interval is wider, and state the trade-off involved.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li><b>Random:</b> the bats are a random sample. <b>Independence:</b> the bat population across hibernation sites is much larger than $10\times640$. <b>Large counts:</b> there are $X=112\ge15$ successes and $n-X=528\ge15$ failures. All conditions are met.</li>
  <li>
  $$\hat{p}=\frac{112}{640}=0.175$$
  $$SE=\sqrt{\frac{(0.175)(0.825)}{640}}=0.0150$$
  $$m=1.960(0.0150)=0.0294$$
  $$0.175\pm0.0294=\boxed{(0.1456,\ 0.2044)}$$
  </li>
  <li>We are $95\%$ confident that between about $14.6\%$ and $20.4\%$ of little brown bats at these hibernation sites show visible signs of white-nose syndrome.</li>
  <li>With $z^*=2.576$:
  $$m=2.576(0.0150)=0.0387$$
  $$0.175\pm0.0387=\boxed{(0.1363,\ 0.2137)}$$
  </li>
  <li>To capture $p$ more often in repeated sampling ($99\%$ instead of $95\%$), the interval needs a larger critical value, so it is wider. The trade-off is between <b>confidence</b> and <b>precision</b>: more confidence means a less precise estimate, unless the sample size is increased.</li>
</ol>

```{r q3-plot, fig.height=2.6}
ci_plot(
  data.frame(method = factor(c("95% CI", "99% CI"), levels = c("99% CI", "95% CI")),
             est = 0.175, lo = c(0.1456, 0.1363), hi = c(0.2044, 0.2137)),
  xlab = "Proportion of bats with white-nose syndrome",
  title = "Higher Confidence, Wider Interval"
)
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $4$

A news report on the bat survey in Question $3$ makes the statements below. For each one, say whether it is correct and explain why.

1. "There is a $95\%$ probability that the true proportion is between $0.1456$ and $0.2044$."
2. "If the survey were repeated many times, about $95\%$ of the intervals calculated this way would contain the true proportion."
3. "The margin of error of $\pm2.9$ percentage points accounts for all sources of error in the survey."
4. "Because a proportion is being estimated, the interval should use $t^*$ with $639$ degrees of freedom instead of $z^*$."
5. "About $17.5\%$ of the bats in the sample showed signs of the disease."

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li><b>Incorrect.</b> Once the interval is calculated, it either contains the fixed value $p$ or it does not. The $95\%$ describes the long-run success rate of the <i>method</i>, not the probability for one calculated interval.</li>
  <li><b>Correct.</b> This is exactly what $95\%$ confidence means (assuming the conditions hold).</li>
  <li><b>Incorrect.</b> The margin of error covers only <i>random sampling</i> variation. It does not cover bias, for example if sick bats are easier or harder to capture, or errors in identifying visible signs of the disease.</li>
  <li><b>Incorrect.</b> For a mean, $t$ is used because a <i>separate</i> parameter $\sigma$ must be estimated by $s$. For a proportion, the spread $p(1-p)/n$ depends only on $p$ itself, so the procedure uses the Normal approximation and $z^*$.</li>
  <li><b>Correct.</b> This describes the sample: $\hat{p}=112/640=0.175$. No inference is needed for a statement about the sample itself.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $5$

Historically, $70\%$ of piping plover eggs on a protected PEI beach hatch successfully. After a season with unusually high storm activity, biologists monitor a random sample of $150$ eggs and find that $93$ hatch. They want to know whether the hatching rate has dropped.

1. State the hypotheses.
2. Check the conditions for the one-proportion $z$ test.
3. Calculate the test statistic.
4. Calculate the $P$-value.
5. State a conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$. Can the biologists conclude that the storms *caused* the change?

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Let $p$ be the proportion of eggs that hatch this season.
  $$H_0:p=0.70\qquad H_a:p<0.70$$
  The alternative is lower-tailed because the question asks whether the rate has <i>dropped</i>.</li>
  <li>The eggs are a random sample, and the expected counts <b>under $H_0$</b> are $np_0=150(0.70)=105\ge10$ and $n(1-p_0)=150(0.30)=45\ge10$. The conditions are met. Eggs in the same nest may not be fully independent, which is a limitation worth noting.</li>
  <li>
  $$\hat{p}=\frac{93}{150}=0.62$$
  $$SE_0=\sqrt{\frac{(0.70)(0.30)}{150}}=0.0374$$
  $$z=\frac{0.62-0.70}{0.0374}=\boxed{-2.138}$$
  Note that the standard error uses $p_0=0.70$, not $\hat{p}$.</li>
  <li>
  $$P=P(Z\le-2.138)\approx\boxed{0.0163}$$
  </li>
  <li>Because $0.0163<0.05$, reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence that the hatching rate this season is below the historical $70\%$.<br>
  The biologists <b>cannot</b> conclude that the storms caused the drop. This is an observational comparison with a historical rate, and other factors that changed this season, such as predators, temperature or human disturbance, could also be responsible.</li>
</ol>

```{r q5-check, echo=TRUE}
p_hat <- 93 / 150
z <- (p_hat - 0.70) / sqrt(0.70 * 0.30 / 150)
c(z = z, p_value = pnorm(z))
```

```{r q5-plot}
g <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800)
q5 <- data.frame(z = g, d = dnorm(g))

ggplot(q5, aes(z, d)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(q5, z <= -2.138), fill = hw_red, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = hw_blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -2.138, linetype = "dashed", colour = hw_red) +
  annotate("text", x = -3.1, y = 0.08, label = "P = 0.0163", colour = hw_red) +
  labs(title = "Lower-Tail P-Value", subtitle = "Observed z = -2.138",
       x = "z", y = "Density") +
  hw_theme
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $6$

Are toads "right-pawed"? A researcher observes a random sample of $60$ cane toads removing a strip of paper from their snouts. $36$ use their right forelimb. If toads have no preference, the proportion using the right forelimb would be $0.5$.

1. State hypotheses to test whether toads have a preference for either side.
2. Calculate the test statistic and the two-sided $P$-value.
3. State a conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
4. Construct a $95\%$ large-sample confidence interval for $p$. Is it consistent with the test?
5. A classmate says, "The test didn't reject, so toads have no paw preference." Explain what is wrong with this statement.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Let $p$ be the proportion of cane toads that use the right forelimb.
  $$H_0:p=0.5\qquad H_a:p\neq0.5$$
  The alternative is two-sided because a preference in <i>either</i> direction counts.</li>
  <li>The expected counts are $60(0.5)=30\ge10$ for each side, so the conditions are met.
  $$\hat{p}=\frac{36}{60}=0.60$$
  $$SE_0=\sqrt{\frac{(0.5)(0.5)}{60}}=0.0645$$
  $$z=\frac{0.60-0.50}{0.0645}=\boxed{1.549}$$
  $$P=2P(Z\ge1.549)\approx\boxed{0.1213}$$
  </li>
  <li>Because $0.1213>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. The data do not give significant evidence of a forelimb preference.</li>
  <li>The observed counts are $36\ge15$ and $24\ge15$.
  $$SE=\sqrt{\frac{(0.60)(0.40)}{60}}=0.0632$$
  $$0.60\pm1.960(0.0632)=\boxed{(0.476,\ 0.724)}$$
  The interval contains $0.5$, which is consistent with failing to reject. (The interval and test use slightly different standard errors, based on $\hat{p}$ and $p_0$ respectively, so they can occasionally disagree when a result is near the cutoff.)</li>
  <li>Failing to reject $H_0$ does not prove $H_0$. The interval shows that values from about $0.48$ up to $0.72$ are all plausible, so a fairly strong right-paw preference has not been ruled out. With only $60$ toads, the study may simply lack the precision to detect a moderate preference. The correct statement is: "The data do not provide convincing evidence of a preference."</li>
</ol>

```{r q6-plot, fig.height=2.6}
ci_plot(
  data.frame(method = factor("95% CI"), est = 0.60, lo = 0.476, hi = 0.724),
  xlab = "Proportion using the right forelimb",
  title = "0.5 Is Inside the Interval",
  subtitle = "Consistent with failing to reject, but a strong preference is still plausible",
  ref = 0.5
)
```
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $7$

A veterinary student tests whether more than $30\%$ of dairy cows in a region have subclinical mastitis. In a random sample of $120$ cows, $45$ test positive. The student's work is shown below.

<div style="background:#f7f9fb;border:1px solid #d8e1e8;border-radius:6px;padding:0.8em 1em;margin:0.8em 0;">
$H_0:\hat{p}=0.30\qquad H_a:\hat{p}>0.30$<br>
$\hat{p}=45/120=0.375$<br>
$SE=\sqrt{0.375(0.625)/120}=0.0442$<br>
$z=(0.375-0.30)/0.0442=1.697$, so $P=0.0449$<br>
"Since $P<0.05$, we have proved that more than $30\%$ of cows have subclinical mastitis."
</div>

1. Identify the error in the hypotheses and correct it.
2. Identify the error in the standard error and recompute it correctly.
3. Recompute the test statistic and $P$-value.
4. Identify the error in the conclusion and rewrite it correctly.
5. The student also wants a $95\%$ confidence interval and plans to use $SE=\sqrt{0.30(0.70)/120}$. Is that correct? Explain.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Hypotheses are always about the <b>parameter</b> $p$, never the statistic $\hat{p}$. We already know $\hat{p}=0.375$, so there is nothing to test about it.
  $$H_0:p=0.30\qquad H_a:p>0.30$$
  </li>
  <li>A test calculates everything assuming $H_0$ is true, so the standard error must use $p_0=0.30$, not $\hat{p}$:
  $$SE_0=\sqrt{\frac{(0.30)(0.70)}{120}}=\boxed{0.0418}$$
  </li>
  <li>
  $$z=\frac{0.375-0.30}{0.0418}=\boxed{1.793}$$
  $$P=P(Z\ge1.793)\approx\boxed{0.0365}$$
  The expected counts $120(0.30)=36$ and $120(0.70)=84$ are both at least $10$, so the test is valid.</li>
  <li>A test never "proves" anything, and a $P$-value just below $0.05$ is moderate evidence, not certainty. A correct conclusion: "Because $P=0.0365<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence that more than $30\%$ of dairy cows in the region have subclinical mastitis."</li>
  <li>No. A confidence interval has <b>no null value</b>, so it uses the observed $\hat{p}$:
  $$SE=\sqrt{\frac{(0.375)(0.625)}{120}}=0.0442$$
  The rule is: <b>test uses $p_0$; interval uses $\hat{p}$</b>. The student mixed the two up in both directions.</li>
</ol>
</div>
</details>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### Question $8$

Public health researchers drag cloths along trails in a random sample of Nova Scotia parks and collect $300$ blacklegged ticks. Laboratory testing finds that $66$ carry *Borrelia burgdorferi*, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease. A report from five years ago estimated that $18\%$ of ticks in the province were infected.

1. **State and plan.** Define $p$, and state hypotheses to test whether the infection rate has changed from $18\%$.
2. **Solve: test.** Check the conditions, then calculate the test statistic and two-sided $P$-value. State the conclusion at $\alpha=0.05$.
3. **Solve: interval.** Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for $p$ and interpret it. Is it consistent with the test?
4. **Compare.** The test in part 2 and the interval in part 3 use different standard errors. State both values and explain why they differ.
5. **Scope.** Ticks were only collected along accessible trails. Explain how this could affect the conclusions, and whether a larger sample would fix the problem.

<details class="solution">
<summary>Show solution</summary>
<div class="solution-body">
<ol>
  <li>Let $p$ be the proportion of blacklegged ticks in Nova Scotia parks that carry <i>B. burgdorferi</i>.
  $$H_0:p=0.18\qquad H_a:p\neq0.18$$
  The alternative is two-sided because the question asks whether the rate has <i>changed</i>, in either direction.</li>
  <li><b>Conditions:</b> the parks were randomly sampled, the tick population is far larger than $3000$, and the expected counts under $H_0$ are $300(0.18)=54\ge10$ and $300(0.82)=246\ge10$.
  $$\hat{p}=\frac{66}{300}=0.22$$
  $$SE_0=\sqrt{\frac{(0.18)(0.82)}{300}}=0.0222$$
  $$z=\frac{0.22-0.18}{0.0222}=\boxed{1.803}$$
  $$P=2P(Z\ge1.803)\approx\boxed{0.0713}$$
  Because $0.0713>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. The data do not give significant evidence at the $5\%$ level that the infection rate has changed from $18\%$, although the sample rate of $22\%$ is suggestive.</li>
  <li>The observed counts are $66\ge15$ and $234\ge15$.
  $$SE=\sqrt{\frac{(0.22)(0.78)}{300}}=0.0239$$
  $$m=1.960(0.0239)=0.0469$$
  $$0.22\pm0.0469=\boxed{(0.173,\ 0.267)}$$
  We are $95\%$ confident that between about $17.3\%$ and $26.7\%$ of ticks in these parks are infected. The interval contains $0.18$, which is consistent with failing to reject. It also shows that rates as high as about $27\%$ are plausible, so a meaningful increase has not been ruled out.</li>
  <li>The test uses $SE_0=0.0222$, and the interval uses $SE=0.0239$. A test assumes $H_0$ is true, so its standard error is calculated under the null value $p_0=0.18$. A confidence interval has no null value, so it can only use the observed $\hat{p}=0.22$. The same reasoning explains why the test's conditions use expected counts ($np_0$, $n(1-p_0)$) while the interval's conditions use observed counts ($X$, $n-X$).</li>
  <li>Ticks along accessible trails may not represent ticks in the wider park, for example in dense forest or leaf litter away from trails. Trail-side habitat may also be visited by different host animals, which could make infection rates higher or lower there. This is <b>selection bias</b>. The results apply most directly to ticks along trails, which is still relevant for hikers. A larger sample would shrink the margin of error, but it would <b>not</b> fix the bias. It would just give a more precise estimate of the wrong population. Fixing the problem requires changing <i>how</i> ticks are sampled, not <i>how many</i>.</li>
</ol>

```{r q8-check, echo=TRUE}
x <- 66; n <- 300; p0 <- 0.18
p_hat <- x / n

# Test (standard error uses p0)
se_null <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
z <- (p_hat - p0) / se_null
c(se_null = se_null, z = z, p_value = 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)))

# Interval (standard error uses p_hat)
se_ci <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
c(se_ci = se_ci, p_hat + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * se_ci)
```

```{r q8-plot, fig.height=2.6}
ci_plot(
  data.frame(method = factor("95% CI"), est = 0.22, lo = 0.173, hi = 0.267),
  xlab = "Proportion of ticks carrying B. burgdorferi",
  title = "The Previous 18% Is Still Plausible",
  subtitle = "Dashed line: earlier estimate of 0.18",
  ref = 0.18
)
```
</div>
</details>
